clue.text: Got the post — it's in the paper

definitions.meaning: someone appointed to an office has had the appointment officially announced
published in an official journal such as the London Gazette

explanation.definitionFit: To be gazetted is to have an appointment published in the official Gazette, so it covers both winning a post and appearing in print.

clue.text: " Time, you old — " (Hodgson)

parts.note: the missing words complete the first line of a poem by Ralph Hodgson addressing Time as a wandering traveller

explanation.walkthrough: Ralph Hodgson's poem 'Time, You Old Gipsy Man' opens with those words; the clue asks for the two missing words.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's title and opening line call Time a roving Romany traveller, which fills the gap.

clue.text: Sway had he, after a Jeroboam!

definitions.text: Sway had he, after a Jeroboam!

parts.words: Sway had he, after a Jeroboam
parts.note: sway means royal rule; the Bible records which king reigned after Jeroboam II of Israel

explanation.surface: A man staggers after downing a huge bottle of champagne.
explanation.walkthrough: A jeroboam is also a large wine bottle, so the surface suggests someone swaying from drink; in 2 Kings 14:29 Jeroboam's son succeeded him on Israel's throne.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical king who succeeded Jeroboam II held sway, that is reigned, over Israel.

clue.text: Wet seasons

definitions.meaning: the sea's rising and falling waters are the wet movements of the shore
an old word for a time of year, as in Christmastide or Eastertide

explanation.definitionFit: The ocean's ebb and flow are watery, and in older English the same word meant a season or festival time.

clue.text: Such as attend summit conferences

parts.note: people who meet at a summit are the high-ranking, and a summit is a lofty point

explanation.surface: Describing the sort of person who goes to top-level talks.
explanation.definitionFit: Distinguished, high-ranking people are those invited to top-level meetings, and the word also means towering like a peak.

clue.text: A maritime Peggotty harboured in Durham

parts.note: maritime means of the sea
Ham Peggotty is the fisherman in Dickens's David Copperfield

explanation.surface: A Dickensian sailor sheltering in a northern English port.
explanation.walkthrough: Ham is the Peggotty who works at sea in David Copperfield. The town is a harbour on the coast of County Durham in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: This County Durham town is built around its harbour, so it is a place harboured in that county.

clue.text: Extends a lone shift at the portals

indicators.note: to shift the letters of the word lone is to move them into a new order

parts.note: portals are doorways or gateways

explanation.surface: A solitary worker puts in extra hours guarding the entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shift' turns LONE into ELON; GATES (portals) follows. The 'a' before 'lone' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: To lengthen something is to stretch or extend it.

clue.text: Harry the French

parts.note: read as the name Harry as the French say it, not a verb meaning to harass

explanation.surface: An order to harass the French troops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry' looks like a verb, to harass; it is the name, given in its French form.
explanation.definitionFit: The French equivalent of the English name Harry (Henry) is the form used for French kings.

clue.text: The plane that's not really there ?

definitions.meaning: a French jet fighter made by Dassault bears this name
an optical illusion, such as water seen in a desert

explanation.definitionFit: The Dassault fighter shares its name with the desert illusion of something that seems present but is not.

clue.text: Rigorous here for the rig

parts.note: a harsh-climate US state where oil rigs work in severe cold

explanation.surface: Conditions on an oil platform are harsh.
explanation.walkthrough: The northern US state is famed for its bitter climate and its oil fields, so life on the rigs there is rigorous.
explanation.definitionFit: The far-northern American state has a severe climate and a large oil industry, fitting a hard place for rig workers.

clue.text: Prepare to be a boring traveller? Poor Atkins !

parts.note: to prepare for a journey is to pack one's bags
boring a hole is drilling it

explanation.surface: A tedious traveller gets ready to leave, and a soldier is pitied.
explanation.walkthrough: Tommy Atkins is the old nickname for a British private soldier; marching up and down in full kit was a punishment for him. 'to be a' and 'traveller' frame the packing.
explanation.definitionFit: Marching in full kit as a military punishment was the lot of the hapless British private, nicknamed Tommy Atkins.

clue.text: Nothing has poor Wren — but he has something

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

indicators.note: poor suggests the word Wren is in a bad state and its letters are mangled

explanation.surface: The architect Christopher Wren is penniless, though he does own something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poor' rearranges WREN to WNER, placed after O; 'has' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who possesses a thing is its proprietor.

clue.text: Locust's grub

parts.note: food for the locust in the Bible, which says it ate up long stretches of time

explanation.walkthrough: Joel 2:25 promises to restore 'the years that the locust hath eaten', so time is what the locust eats.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Book of Joel the locust devours time measured in twelve-month spans.

clue.text: Mood of the primrose path

parts.note: the primrose path is the pleasant road of indulgence, so its spirit is relaxed travel

explanation.surface: Describing the spirit of a life of pleasure.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'primrose path' (from Hamlet) is a life of easy pleasure; the going on such a path is easy, which is also a relaxed mood.
explanation.definitionFit: A relaxed, tolerant temperament matches the smooth, pleasant progress of the primrose path.

clue.text: The factor can be made to quail

indicators.note: the words to quail can be made into something else by rearranging them

explanation.surface: A powerful agent can make someone cower in fear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be made' rearranges TO QUAIL. 'quail' looks like the verb to cower, but it is just fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A number that divides another exactly is an exact part of it, which mathematicians call a factor.

clue.text: Browne's theme of " the iniquity of oblivion"

definitions.text: Browne's theme of " the iniquity of oblivion"

parts.words: Browne's theme of " the iniquity of oblivion"
parts.note: Sir Thomas Browne wrote of how oblivion scatters her poppy in his essay on ancient funeral urns

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase comes from Sir Thomas Browne's Hydriotaphia, a 1658 essay prompted by Roman funeral urns dug up in Norfolk.
explanation.definitionFit: Browne's essay on burying cremated remains in vessels is the source of the quoted line, so its subject is the answer.

clue.text: Fix in friendship

definitions.meaning: to fix something on is to fasten it
to bind someone to oneself by affection or loyalty

explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to fasten physically and to bind someone by affection, as in becoming fond of a friend.

clue.text: Imperial originator of the baths

parts.note: a Roman emperor who built the great public baths in Rome that bear his name

explanation.surface: An emperor credited with founding a bathhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: The great Roman baths, still standing and used for opera, were built under the emperor whose nickname they bear.
explanation.definitionFit: This third-century Roman emperor commissioned the huge public baths named after him.

clue.text: Easy money? Seems not

parts.note: the opposite of easy is hard, so money described by that opposite word

explanation.walkthrough: Hard is the opposite of easy, and the phrase means actual coins and notes.
explanation.definitionFit: Physical money in coins and notes is called by a phrase whose first word is the opposite of easy.

clue.text: Just Conrad's luck !

definitions.meaning: the title of Joseph Conrad's 1913 novel

explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Conrad's 1913 novel has this title, and the word also means fortune or luck.

clue.text: Praises with any number of bells ?

definitions.text: Praises with any number of bells

parts.words: Praises with any number of bells
parts.note: x stands for any number, and bells toll, so the word reads as x tolls

explanation.walkthrough: In algebra x stands for any number; said out, the answer is 'x tolls', an unknown number of bell strokes.
explanation.definitionFit: To praise highly is to laud, and the word sounds like an unknown number of bell peals.

clue.text: Scene of a landau's trial trip

indicators.note: of signals the letters are taken out of the run of words landau's trial

explanation.surface: Where a new horse-drawn carriage was taken for its test run.
explanation.walkthrough: A landau is a four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage. The country is in landAU'S TRIAl; 'a' and 'trip' complete the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A country is a setting where events take place, a scene.

clue.text: Go-slow adopted by scores

parts.note: a go-slow is a work protest, but here it is a slow speed marked in musical scores

explanation.surface: Many workers take part in a go-slow protest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scores' looks like large numbers of people; it means sheets of music, where an Italian marking asks for a moderately slow pace.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian musical direction asks players for a walking, moderately slow pace.

clue.text: Little girl lost-grimmish

parts.note: a small girl lost in the woods in a tale collected by the Brothers Grimm

explanation.walkthrough: 'grimmish' points to the Brothers Grimm, whose tale has a brother and sister lost in a forest.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Grimms' fairy tale the girl and her brother are abandoned in the woods and lost.

clue.text: Fortified post the newspaperman finds formidable

parts.note: a redoubt is a small fortification
ED is short for editor, the newspaperman in charge

explanation.surface: A journalist finds an army stronghold intimidating.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic adjective for someone feared or dreaded, hence formidable.

clue.text: To make civil, put far from the madding crowd ?

definitions.meaning: to release a soldier back into civilian life

definitions.text: put far from the madding crowd
definitions.meaning: de- means away from, and mob is a crowd, so the word reads as away from the mob

explanation.definitionFit: Releasing troops into civilian life is a de-mob, which can be read as taking someone away from the mob.

clue.text: Made tight, having mixed one's drink

definitions.meaning: fastened with laces, like a corset

explanation.definitionFit: A corset or shoe drawn tight with cords, and a drink with alcohol added, share the word.

clue.text: Pull up, sailor, before revealing identity of the one you deceive

definitions.meaning: a nautical term for a ship stopping and holding position

definitions.text: before revealing identity of the one you deceive
definitions.meaning: the words that come before the name of someone you deceive

explanation.definitionFit: Sailors use the phrase for halting a ship head to wind, and it also means to deceive someone whose name follows.

clue.text: The Musical Times

parts.note: the title of a music journal, read as the speeds at which music is played

explanation.walkthrough: The Musical Times is a long-running British magazine; read literally, it asks for the plural of an Italian word for musical speed.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian plural for musical speeds means times in music.

clue.text: Apple-growing was no straightforward affair here for a poet

definitions.text: Apple-growing was no straightforward affair here for a poet

parts.words: Apple-growing was no straightforward affair here for a poet
parts.note: William Barnes's poem describes an apple tree that leans down low in a Dorset place

explanation.surface: A poet found it hard to grow apples somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: William Barnes's song says 'the apple tree do lean down low' there, so the apples did not grow straight.
explanation.definitionFit: The place in William Barnes's Dorset poem has an apple tree that leans rather than grows upright.

clue.text: Categorizers

parts.note: things that sort items into classes, such as tags on goods

explanation.definitionFit: Tags fixed to items assign them to a category.

clue.text: "I silently laugh at my own "(Shelley)

parts.note: a line from Shelley's poem The Cloud, missing its last word, a monument to someone buried elsewhere

explanation.walkthrough: In Shelley's 'The Cloud' the cloud laughs at the blue sky, its empty tomb, since it is always reborn.
explanation.definitionFit: The empty-tomb monument completes Shelley's line, the sky being a memorial with no body beneath.
